summary: Examines a possible lockup, or deadlock, in the IMP subnet caused by message sequencing. It explains that protocols must be designed carefully to avoid lockups, which usually show up only in unforeseen circumstances.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 626 analyzes a possible deadlock in the IMP subnet caused by message sequencing and buffer allocation. It proposes reserving buffer space for single-packet messages to prevent the described cycle.

questions: how could message sequencing deadlock the imp subnet
subtitle: A possible deadlock caused by message order and shared IMP buffers.

tldr.problem: The authors describe a possible IMP subnet lockup in which buffers allocated to out-of-order multi-packet messages could prevent the next single-packet messages from being delivered.
tldr.mechanism: The scenario combines sequencing, a shared pool of reassembly buffers and allocations piggy-backed on RFNMs for the next multi-packet message.
tldr.outcome: The authors propose reserving a reassembly buffer for single-packet messages so the described lockup cannot occur.

facts.label: Packet count in each large message

today: RFC 626 is an analysis of a possible IMP subnet deadlock and a proposed buffer-allocation safeguard.

sections.title: Why Message Sequencing Can Lock Up
sections.content:
The authors examine a possible deadlock in the IMP subnet that they say had not been observed. Messages leave a destination IMP in the order they entered the source IMP. A message that arrives out of order may use buffers needed by an earlier message, preventing the earlier message from being delivered and blocking later messages in turn.

The concern arises from a buffer allocation piggy-backed on an RFNM for a multi-packet message: it allocates for the next multi-packet message, not necessarily the next message in sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages must be delivered in order, but later messages can occupy buffers needed by an earlier one. The authors explain how this could leave every message waiting for resources held by another.

sections.title: The Example Deadlock
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example with IMPs A, B and C sending eight-packet messages to IMP D, using all 24 of D's reassembly buffers. Each IMP then sends a single-packet message. When buffers become free, piggy-backed allocations can assign them to the next multi-packet messages instead. Those messages are out of order and cannot be delivered, while the single-packet messages that should go first cannot get buffers.

The authors say the scenario is unlikely, but note that similar problems could occur with other buffer counts and that the current maximum number of buffers was 58.
sections.plainLanguage: In the example, all buffers go to large messages that cannot be delivered yet because earlier single-packet messages are waiting. The single-packet messages cannot move forward because they have no buffers.

sections.title: Reserve Buffer Space for Single-Packet Messages
sections.content: The proposed safeguard is to set aside one reassembly buffer, or one for each destination host, for single-packet messages only. The authors say this breaks the described lockup condition. They also mention moving sequencing to the host level or discontinuing multi-packet messages, but describe those alternatives as requiring broader coordination or more extensive changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep buffer space available only for single-packet messages. Then a message that must go next can still be accepted even when other buffers are occupied.
